text:
===== FILE 2601__1.pdf =====
Federal Register Comment 
Submitter: Ilan Adona 
Date: August 12, 2025 
 
Proposed Rule: 
Reproductive Health Services 
A Proposed Rule by the Department of Veterans Affairs on August 4, 2025 
Docket No. 2025-14687, 90 Fed. Reg. 36415 
 
The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is proposing to “reinstate the full exclusion on 
abortions and abortion counseling from the medical benefits package” that was previously 
removed in 2022 (Reproductive Health Services, 2025). This regulatory decision is based 
on the determination that abortions are not a “needed” service (Reproductive Health 
Services, 2025). This is concerning to me as a United States citizen and as a woman 
because I believe that abortion and abortion counseling are needed as much as most other 
available and VA covered medical procedures and counseling. I recommend this proposed 
rule be discarded because it is unnecessary, and the process of reinstating the rule is a 
drain on VA resources. Based on the research provided in the proposed rule and outside 
research, there is no clear benefit to reinstating the abortion exclusion. 
The proposed rule cites the VA prediction from the September 9, 2022 Interim Final 
Rule and March 4, 2024 Final Rule that the “VA would provide abortions to more than 1,000 
veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries per year,” but in actuality the “average number of 
veterans who receive abortions from the VA is 100 per year, and the average number of 
CHAMPVA beneficiaries who receive abortions from the VA is 40 per year” (Reproductive 
Health Services, 2025). Additionally, the VA states in its proposed rule that the “VA has 
never understood this policy to prohibit providing care to pregnant women in life-
threatening circumstances, including treatment for ectopic pregnancies or 
miscarriages....” and goes on to state that they will provide abortion services in those 
situations (Reproductive Health Services, 2025). These facts matter for three reasons: 1) 
The data of VA performed abortions do not delineate between those women electing 
abortions due to life threatening conditions or for another reason. 2) The VA is providing 
over 90 percent fewer abortions than anticipated and has made clear that they would 
continue performing abortions in certain situations. 3) Pregnancy is inherently a potentially 

life-threatening condition. According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) February 
2023 Health E-Stats, 817 women died from maternal causes in 2022 and 669 died from 
maternal causes in 2023 (2023 Health E-Stats, 2025). According to this data, the number of 
abortions performed by the VA is highly unlikely to decrease even in the slightest with this 
proposed rule and therefore, the rule is unnecessary. 
According to the Department of Defense’s (DoD) 2023 Demographics Profile of the 
Military Community, 19.7% of the total military in 2023 were female (Demographics Profile 
of the Military Community, 2023). The proposed rule states several times that the 
determining factor for excluding abortions and abortion counseling in the VA’s medical 
plan is that the services are not “needed.” It is true that abortions are not “needed” by 
80.3% of the military who are male, but this diminishes the possible medical needs of 
almost a fifth of the entire military. Under CHAMPVA and VA medical coverage, many 
covered services credibly fall under the not “needed” category defined by this proposed 
rule because they are elective. In fact, the following are examples of elective services and 
procedures provided by CHAMPVA medical coverage: wigs or hairpieces, penile implants, 
weight loss medication, genetic testing, tubal ligations, and vasectomies (CHAMPVA 
Guidebook, 2025). There is no specific ban on elective services or procedures under VA 
guidelines, so it is unclear why abortions and abortion counseling should be excluded, 
especially when the service is infrequently performed. The proposed rule cites 
dissatisfaction pertaining to “forced taxpayer funding” as a specific reason to exclude 
abortions, but I cannot imagine that taxpayers are any more sympathetic to “forced 
taxpayer funding” for penile implants, vasectomies, or weight loss medication 
(Reproductive Health Services, 2025). 
The Reproductive Health Services proposed rule costs are a drain on VA resources. 
Abortions are not particularly expensive. According to Planned Parenthood, abortions cost 
anywhere from $600 to $2,000 depending on the type of abortion (How much does an 
abortion cost?, 2025). Although this is the cost for patients, if estimating on the high end of 
100 abortions per year at $2,000 per abortion, the VA is averaging $200,000 per year. As the 
above data depicts, the majority of these abortions will be performed by the VA regardless 
if this proposed rule is implemented or not because they will be performed in life 
threatening situations. Meanwhile, at the time of writing this comment, the Reproductive 
Health Services proposed rule has received 2,597 comments and this number will likely 
increase before the September 3, 2025 comment deadline (Reproductive Health Services, 
2025). Pursuant to Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 553(c), the VA is required to 
consider each of the comments and even incorporate the considerations into the Final 
Rule (Administrative Procedure Act, 2023). The average salary of a VA employee is 
$105,765 (govsalaries.com, 2024). If four employees spend three months reviewing and 

incorporating comments into the Final Rule, that task alone will cost the government over 
$100,000, which is significant at a time when agency staffing and budgets are decreased. 
Given it is likely that regardless of whether this proposed rule is implemented or not, the VA 
will continue to perform on average of 100 abortions a year, the expense of this process is 
futile. 
I would also like to comment on the misleading title of this proposed rule - 
“Reproductive Health Services.” This title does two things. First, it suggests this proposed 
rule is about providing reproductive health services to military families, personnel, and 
veterans. The opposite it true as it proposes to remove reproductive health services from 
beneficiaries that they have previously had access to. Secondly, the title deems abortion 
and abortion counseling as reproductive health services, which suggests they are in fact 
needed as part of the whole array of other reproductive, pre-natal, and post-natal services 
provided by the VA. Language matters. The purpose of this proposed rule, to remove 
reproductive health services from beneficiaries' coverage, is hidden behind the seemingly 
innocuous, even positive title.  
Please consider discarding the Reproductive Health Services proposed rule in light 
of the data and the purpose of the VA’s medical coverage. As stated in the proposed rule, 
abortions are a reproductive health service that are often necessary. Unlike abortion 
services, this proposed rule is unnecessary and a financial burden on the VA.
